title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, which is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.
shortTitle: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree: recursive DFS
keyPoints: Maximum depth is 1 plus the greater of the left and right subtree depths, with null returning 0
This is a post-order computation because a parent needs both children's answers first
Time is O(n) visiting every node once; space is O(h) for the recursion stack
For a balanced tree h is O(log n); for a skewed tree h is O(n) risking stack overflow
An iterative BFS alternative counts levels and avoids deep recursion on pathological trees
The same pattern applies to measuring the longest escalation chain in any hierarchical system

s1_definition.oneliner: The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its two children, and a null child contributes zero.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Maximum Depth** is the number of nodes along the longest root-to-leaf path in a binary tree.
- **Recursive formula** is `1 + Math.max(depth(left), depth(right))` with `depth(null) = 0`.
- **Post-order style** means the parent cannot compute its depth until both children have reported theirs.
- **Time** is O(n) because every node is visited exactly once.
- **Space** is O(h) for the call stack, where h is the tree height.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's loan approval hierarchy as a tree, with the branch manager at the top and reporting chains going down. The maximum depth is the longest chain of command from the manager down to the most junior clerk. Each manager asks their two deputies how deep their sub-teams go, takes the deeper answer, and adds one for themselves. The number that bubbles up to the top is the longest chain in the whole branch.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Post-order depth computation
  ============================

  Tree:        1
              / \
             2    3
            /
           4

  Call order (post-order):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  maxDepth(4.left=null) → 0        │
  │  maxDepth(4.right=null) → 0       │
  │  maxDepth(4) = 1 + max(0,0) = 1   │
  │  maxDepth(2.right=null) → 0       │
  │  maxDepth(2) = 1 + max(1,0) = 2   │
  │  maxDepth(3.left=null) → 0        │
  │  maxDepth(3.right=null) → 0       │
  │  maxDepth(3) = 1 + max(0,0) = 1   │
  │  maxDepth(1) = 1 + max(2,1) = 3   │
  └────────────────────────────────────┘

  Formula at each node:
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ null → 0     │
  │ else →       │
  │  1 + max(L,R)│
  └──────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree is the cleanest example of a recursive definition that translates directly into code. The depth of any node is one plus the greater of its two subtree depths, and a null node returns zero. This three-line recursion visits every node once in post-order style, because a parent cannot know its depth until both children have reported theirs.

Taking the maximum of the two sides guarantees you measure the longest root-to-leaf path, and treating a missing child as zero makes unbalanced and empty trees fall out correctly without special cases. The time is O(n) and the space is O(h) for the call stack.

For very deep trees, the recursive approach risks a StackOverflowError on the default Java stack size, so the senior-level alternative is an iterative BFS that counts levels using a queue. Knowing when to prefer the stack-safe form over the elegant recursive form is what distinguishes a production engineer from someone who only knows textbook solutions.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to measure the longest escalation chain in a loan approval hierarchy. A chain that is too deep means a loan takes too many hops and breaches the service-level agreement, so the recursion returns the longest chain length and the service raises a warning when it exceeds the threshold.

Remember one sentence: maximum depth is `1 + max(left, right)` with null returning zero, and that three-line recursion is the foundation for every post-order tree computation.
